t: Marx and Engels gave communism its modern definition in The Communist Manifesto of 1848: a classless society, reached through proletarian revolution, in which goods would be shared according to need.

From the Russian Revolution of 1917 Communist governments spread to Eastern Europe, Asia and other regions, and for much of the 20th century more than one-third of the world’s population lived under them.

Communist states were marked by one-party rule, state control of the economy and the media, and the suppression of opposition; estimates of the deaths under them range from 10–20 million to over 100 million and remain disputed.
dyk: One of the first uses of the word in its modern sense is in a letter of around 1785 in which Victor d’Hupay called himself an auteur communiste, a “communist author”.
ev: Nicolas Restif de la Bretonne uses communisme for a social order based on equality and the common ownership of property
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish The Communist Manifesto, offering a new definition of communism
The October Revolution brings Lenin’s Bolsheviks to power in Russia, the first avowedly communist party to take state power
The Bolsheviks found the Comintern, dedicated to promoting revolution throughout the world
Stalin’s Great Purge begins; in the Moscow trials leading old Bolsheviks are accused, plead guilty to conspiracy and are executed
Mao Zedong and the Chinese Communist Party come to power in China at the end of the Chinese Civil War
Mao’s Cultural Revolution begins, a ten-year upheaval that targets intellectuals and party leaders
The Soviet Union is dissolved, after the Revolutions of 1989 have brought down most of the Eastern Bloc

f.thinkers: François-Noël Babeuf, Nicolas Restif de la Bretonne and Sylvain Maréchal, in James H. Billington’s view the progenitors of modern communism; Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, founders of Marxism; Vladimir Lenin, theorist of the vanguard party; Joseph Stalin, who developed Marxism–Leninism; Leon Trotsky, of permanent revolution; Mao Zedong; Peter Kropotkin, main theorist of anarcho-communism
f.texts: Thomas More’s Utopia (1516), an early picture of common ownership; The Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels (1848); Friedrich Engels’s The Peasant War in Germany (1850); Eduard Bernstein’s Cromwell and Communism (1895); Marx’s Grundrisse and The Civil War in France, on which libertarian Marxists draw
f.ideas: common ownership of the means of production, distribution and exchange; class struggle between the proletariat and the bourgeoisie; historical materialism; the dictatorship of the proletariat as the transition; distribution “from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs”; the end of social classes, money and the state
f.today: as of 2026 China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea and Vietnam are ruled by Communist parties under single-party systems, all but North Korea allowing more economic competition; Communist parties have shared power democratically in Nepal and sit in governing coalitions in Brazil and Uruguay; the Progressive Party of the Working People won 22.3% of the vote in Cyprus in 2026; remnants of Peru’s Shining Path are still active
